head:
Parents · Child aged 6 to 11

My child is out of shape: where to start?

Your child gets out of breath quickly, finishes last in running games, prefers the screen to the park. You wonder whether you should make them “train”. The research answers differently: at this age, you do not set up a training plan. You make room for play, motor skills and sleep, and you do it together, over a long time. The plan below is written for you, the parent, and it reads in games and habits, not in sessions.

The question

The question

A child aged 6 to 11 is out of shape. What can you do in practice, without turning them into either a patient or a little athlete, and how do you know when to ask for medical advice?

To set out the problem, let's take a child aged 8. This is an illustrative profile, not a real person. They like cartoons and video games. In PE at school, they do not like running, because they often come in behind the others. They are sometimes a little round. They fall asleep late. Their parents see that they tire faster than their cousins and hesitate between three answers: signing them up for a sport, “putting them on a diet”, or waiting for it to pass.

Each of these three answers can go wrong. A sport chosen without them can reinforce the idea that they are “not gifted”. A diet decided about their body can damage their relationship with themselves. Waiting lets habits settle in that will become slower to change. The aim of this article is to give you a fourth way, based on what has been measured.

What is at stake

What is at stake is not performance. It is the place movement will take in your child's life. A child who feels competent in the basic movements (running, jumping, throwing, catching) has reasons to move. A child who feels clumsy has fewer and fewer, and steps away from the games in which they could improve. We will see later that a follow-up study links these two things.7

There is also a collective issue, which concerns you without being your fault. According to Santé publique France, in the Esteban study (2014-2016), only half of boys and a third of girls met the WHO physical activity recommendations, with no improvement since 2006-2007, and with daily screen time sharply up.16 Your child is therefore not an exception: the current context pushes towards staying still. It is not a failing on your part or theirs.

Finally, there is an opposite risk, which needs to be named: turning a lack of fitness into a weight problem, and then into a source of shame. The Haute Autorité de santé (HAS) writes that preventing and fighting stigmatisation is “essential”.4 Everything that follows is built so that your child is never the subject of the problem, but a member of the family who changes habits along with the others.

What changes with the profile, and what does not

The core of a fitness plan is the same at every age: a little regular volume, strength, progression, a measurement, recovery. For a child aged 6 to 11, what changes is the starting point (play, not the session), the dose (an average of 60 minutes a day, all movement included), what you avoid (dieting, comparisons, taking the timer seriously), the obstacles (the parent organises the day) and the moments when medical advice is needed.

What the research says for this profile

Step 1. What the THW tests for children measure, and what they do not

The Decaform Kids 8-10 and 11-12 tests each include seven tests, each scored by age, for a total out of 1,000 points. They cover different qualities, and that is their value: they show where the gap lies, not just that it exists.

20 m shuttle runEndurance: how long they last at an increasing pace. Included in both tests.
10 × 5 m shuttleSpeed and coordination when changing direction.
30 m sprintRunning speed over a short distance.
Standing long jumpLeg power, arm-leg coordination.
Shoulder tap (8-10 years) or knee push-ups and foot tap (11-12 years)Plank, upper-body strength, coordination.
Burpees without push-up (8-10 years)Explosive cardio, child version.
Flamingo balance (8-10 years)Balance on one leg, time held with a ceiling of 45 seconds.
Strength + cardio circuit (11-12 years)Muscular endurance, strength and coordination, three rounds.

These tests measure neither weight, nor health, nor talent. They do not replace the body-size growth chart in the health record book, which only a professional can interpret.4 The THW test starts at age 8. For a child of 6 or 7, none of the tests in the series applies: instead you observe, in the form of games, whether they can throw and catch a ball, hop on one foot, stand on one leg, run without tripping over their own feet. This is a suggestion, not a norm table.

The 20 m shuttle run has one advantage: it is the test from which a large meta-analysis estimated young people's endurance (965,264 children and adolescents aged 9 to 17, 19 countries, between 1981 and 2014). According to it, endurance (cardiorespiratory fitness) fell by 3.3 mL/kg/min on average, or 7.3%.15 mL/kg/min is the unit of maximal oxygen uptake, relative to body weight. Simply remember that it is a measure of endurance, and that it has fallen.

The decline in young people's endurance has slowed markedly since the 2000s

Values per decade as reported by the meta-analysis. Source: Tomkinson et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2019.15

What this means

These young people are not doomed to lose endurance: the fall was steep in the 1980s and 1990s, then almost stopped. But this study covers 9-17 year olds in mostly rich countries, and the population as a whole, not your child. It says that the context has changed, not that your child is doing badly. Only their own result, retested over time, answers your question.

The first step is therefore set: the test is there to place your child and to retest them, never to grade them. The next one concerns the dose: how much to move, and in what form.

Step 2. A child is not a small adult: the dose is counted in play

The WHO, in its 2020 guidelines, recommends that 5-17 year olds do an average of at least 60 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous intensity physical activity, mostly aerobic, across the week. It adds at least three days a week of vigorous activities and of activities that strengthen muscles and bones. It also asks to limit time spent sitting, in particular recreational screen time. The first two recommendations are strong with moderate certainty of evidence; the third is strong with low certainty of evidence, and no numerical limit is given.1

Three words matter in this sentence. “Average”: one day at 30 minutes and another at 90 make 60. “All included”: break time, cycling, the walk to school, games in the park, PE all count. “Strengthen muscles and bones”: jumping, climbing, pushing, pulling, running all count, with no gym. It is not a programme, it is a volume of life.

Strength is not off-limits at this age. The 2014 international consensus on youth strength training judges that the fears about growth plates are not supported. It asks for programmes supervised by qualified professionals, which prioritise technique, and recommends low volume and intensity for beginners. It also notes that overweight young people get injured more than twice as often, often because of lower postural stability.14 For you, this translates without equipment: bodyweight games, with an adult nearby, built on technique before adding effort.

What this means

The 60-minute bar is an average target over the week, reached in small touches. It does not require your child to “do sport”: it requires their day to include movement. That is what makes the plan accessible to a child who does not like organised sport.

One question remains that every parent asks: is being out of shape a weight problem? Not necessarily, and the answer changes how you act.

Step 3. Weight: a family approach, never the child's body as the target

A child can be out of shape without being overweight, and an overweight child can be active. When overweight is present, the HAS (2022 recommendation) calls for comprehensive care. The family is made aware and supported, the project is built with the child and their parents, sedentary behaviours, notably screens, are reduced, and regular physical activity is resumed. Weight loss is not the priority, except in the case of complications: in a growing child, the aim is to slow weight gain while growth continues.4 According to a press report on the HAS, the prevalence would be 17% overweight and 4% obesity among children over 6.5 Overweight is therefore common: your child is not alone, and the family should not feel at fault.

How well do programmes that treat overweight work? The Cochrane review by Mead and colleagues (2017) gathered 70 controlled trials, 8,461 children aged 6 to 11, followed from six months to three years. Almost all of them (64 out of 70) combined diet, physical activity and behaviour change. At the longest follow-up, the mean change in BMI z-score is minus 0.06, that in BMI minus 0.53 kg/m², and that in weight minus 1.45 kg compared with the comparison groups. The certainty of evidence is rated low to very low. The authors speak of a small short-term reduction and acknowledge that it is poorly understood how to maintain the effects after the programme ends.2,3

A surprising point: 65 trials out of 70 involved the parents, and the analysis found no difference depending on whether the parents took part or not. The authors also do not explain the variation in results between trials.3,2 This does not prove that parents are useless: almost all the trials included them, so the comparison is not very informative. But it rules out promising that “parental involvement guarantees the result”.

The historical reference for the family approach comes from Epstein. A University at Buffalo press release (1995) describes the ten-year follow-up of 113 families: a child aged 8 to 12 who was 20 to 100% overweight, with at least one obese parent, the parents following the same programme (regular activity, behaviour modification, eating by calorie levels). At ten years, more than 20% of the children kept a 20% reduction in their overweight, against less than 1% of the adults. The children's weight had stabilised at about 7% below the starting point, whereas the adults' weight had returned to the starting line at five years, then to about 7% above at ten years.6

Ten years later, the children in the family programme held on better than their parents

Approximate values read from a university press release (113 families, children aged 8 to 12, obese parents). This is not the original scientific paper. Source: University at Buffalo, 1995.6

What this means

A growing child can stabilise their weight over the long term with a family programme, whereas the adults in the same programme regain it. But this trial is old, it involves volunteer families with marked overweight, and the 2017 Cochrane review recalls it: the average results are modest and poorly understood. What to take away: treat the child within their family, over time, rather than treating them alone or over a month.

One last point on this subject: food is a separate topic, which falls to the doctor or a dietitian. The plan below does not discuss it, because the THW tests do not measure it and we have not read a sufficient source to give you dietary guidance. For now, keep a single rule: never put your child “on a diet” on your own initiative.

Step 4. Coordination: do not skip it

When you want to “get a child back in shape”, you think of endurance and weight, and forget coordination. This is a mistake that the research corrects in two ways.

First, motor skills and fitness go together. A meta-analysis of 13 studies, 27 samples and 15,101 participants (aged 4.5 to 20.4) finds a correlation of 0.48 between motor competence and fitness, described as moderate to strong. Age does not significantly modify the relationship.8 A correlation is not a cause: a fit child may also be more at ease in movements. And the source read is a conference abstract (2018), not the full paper.

Next, motor competence predicts what follows. Barnett and colleagues reassessed in adolescence (16.4 years on average) 276 young people who had been assessed as children at school, six to seven years earlier. Object-control skills (kicking, catching, overhand throwing) in childhood were linked to adolescent physical activity and fitness, through an intermediary: perceived sports competence. The model explains 18% of the variation in activity and 30% of that in fitness; it is the same for boys and girls.7

What this means

A child who feels able to throw, catch and run is more likely to want to move in adolescence. It is not a guarantee: 18% of variation explained is a real link but far from a total one. And it is an observed association, not proof that training these movements improves activity afterwards. In practice: going through skills, and not only through endurance, is the most logical way to make movement enjoyable, and therefore lasting.

Competence is not built through humiliation. A child who fails in front of others in PE class mostly learns to avoid sport. This guides everything that follows: small successful challenges, among themselves, before challenges in front of others.

Step 5. Sleep and screens: an often-forgotten lever

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (2016 consensus) recommends that children aged 6 to 12 sleep 9 to 12 hours per 24 hours, on a regular basis. It associates regularly insufficient sleep with difficulties in attention and learning, and with a higher risk of accidents, hypertension, obesity, diabetes and depression.11 These are associations, and the consensus specifies that a parent who is worried about too much or too little sleep should consult a health professional.

On weight, a meta-analysis by Cappuccio and colleagues (12 studies, 30,002 children) finds an odds ratio of 1.89 between short sleep and obesity in children: children who sleep little are about twice as likely to be obese.13 Association, again: this figure does not tell us whether lack of sleep causes weight gain, or the reverse, or another common factor.

Why talk about screens here? Because they come into the bedroom. A review of 20 studies, more than 125,000 children aged 6 to 19 (mean age about 15), links the use of a device in the 90 minutes before bedtime to insufficient, poorer-quality sleep and to daytime sleepiness. A device in the bedroom, even without using it, is also associated with poorer sleep.12 The press release does not give precise odds ratios, and the mean age is higher than your child's. In France, 3-17 year olds spend on average 3 hours a day in front of screens (ONAPS, 2017, cited by the Fédération française de cardiologie).17

Sixty minutes of activity fit into a day where sleep already takes half

Recommendations: WHO 2020 (activity) and AASM 2016 consensus (sleep). Proportions calculated by us, not from the source.1,11

What this means

The plan does not ask you to “find time” in an already full day: it asks you to move a little screen and sitting time towards movement and towards bedtime. The simplest and best-supported step from these studies: no screen in the bedroom, and a regular bedtime.

Real obstacles and how to remove them

The first obstacle is the family's schedule

A child aged 6 to 11 decides neither their schedule, nor their journey, nor their evening routine. What you change, they follow. A meta-analysis by Yao and Rhodes (2015, 115 studies) shows that parental support (enrolment, transport, encouragement, doing it together) is associated with children's activity (correlation of 0.38), more than simply setting an example (0.16). The authors note strong differences between studies. Above all, the correlation is higher when activity is self-reported (0.46) than when it is measured (0.20).9

Parental support matters, but its weight is more modest when activity is measured

Correlation coefficients (r) from the meta-analysis abstract, 115 studies. A correlation is not an effect. Source: Yao and Rhodes, IJBNPA, 2015.9

What this means

A parent who accompanies their child has a more active child, but the strength of the link falls when it is measured objectively. So do not make your child the result of your efforts: you create conditions, and they move or they do not. In practical terms, what is probably most useful is also the least costly: offer, accompany, and let the child choose. An Australian study of 775 children aged 10-12, whose activity was measured by accelerometer, found that parental modelling and support were associated in different ways depending on the behaviours; its authors only suggest testing these leads.10

The second obstacle is duration

Many families try for a month, see little change, and stop. The study by Lally and colleagues (2010) followed 96 adult students who repeated a new behaviour every day for 84 days: maximum automaticity was reached in 66 days on average, with a range from 18 to 254 days (the latter figure is an extrapolation). Exercise behaviours took about one and a half times longer than eating or drinking behaviours. Missing a single day changed the course very little.18 This study is about adults; for children, it is an indication of duration, not a measurement.

Two tools have a solid basis. First the “if... then”: deciding in advance when, where and how. A meta-analysis by Gollwitzer and Sheeran (2006, 94 independent tests) finds a medium-to-large effect (d = 0.65) on goal attainment when this kind of plan is formulated.19 Then monitoring: the meta-regression by Michie and colleagues (2009, 122 evaluations, 44,747 participants, healthy eating and activity) finds an effect of 0.42 when self-monitoring is combined with at least one other technique, against 0.26 without it.20 It does not focus specifically on children.

What this means

Motivation does not hold on its own. What holds is a system: a time and a place decided in advance (“on Wednesdays, after school, we go to the park”), simple monitoring (a calendar where you tick), and the idea that a missed day hardly counts. Count in months, not in weeks.

The third obstacle is the child themselves

A child who is ashamed of their body or their level will not follow a plan presented as a correction. That said, we have not read an intervention study that measures the effect of this or that wording on the child: what follows is a suggestion based on the position of the HAS (avoid stigmatisation) and on the role of the sense of competence seen above.4,7 Talk about “what we do together” and not “what you must change”. Do not comment on their weight or their speed. Let them choose between two or three games. Present the test as a challenge with themselves (“how many levels next time?”), not as a grade.

And what about school, and clubs?

We have not read a source giving, for 6-11 year olds, the share of school and clubs in the daily 60 minutes. The WHO counts all activity in the average.1 School sport is therefore not enough in principle to reach the dose, and neither should it be set aside: it is part of it. For a child who is out of shape, the logic of competence suggests looking for an activity or a club where they can succeed at movements at their level, with leaders trained for this age, rather than the most “high-performing” sport. A trial session before enrolling is a good rule. This is a suggestion.

The action plan in phases

This plan is a generic twelve-week trajectory, not a tailored programme. It has not been tested as it stands on children: the suggestions are marked as such. Only the recommendations on WHO activity, sleep and the supervision of strength training rest on the studies cited above. It reads in habits and games.

The plan climbs in ten-minute steps, up to the recommended average

Starting values and steps chosen to illustrate: they do not come from any trial. Only the 60-minute line comes from the WHO 2020.1

Week 0 · Starting point

Measure without judging

  • THW test (Kids 8-10 or 11-12). As a game, at home or in the park, with only one parent present. For a child of 6 or 7, observation of movements (throwing, catching, jumping, holding balance), a suggestion without a norm table.
  • Note down a typical week. How many minutes of movement per day, how much screen time, what time bedtime is. No reproach: just a record.
  • Medical advice if a warning sign exists (see below) before increasing effort.
Weeks 1 to 4

Making movement normal

  • Habit. Add 10 minutes of movement on average per day, through an “if... then” written on the fridge: “If we come home from school, then we do 15 minutes outside before screens.” Choose a single ritual, not five.
  • Games. Two outings at home or in the park: chase, ball games (throwing, catching), scooter or bike, jump rope or hopscotch. A game, not an exercise.
  • Less sitting. A standing break during long periods in front of the screen; no screen in the bedroom and a regular bedtime (the window of 9 to 12 hours of sleep is a reference point).
  • Monitoring. A calendar where the child sticks a sticker on days with movement. A missed day is not made up, it is skipped.
  • Move on when the ritual holds almost the whole week, without protest. Step back a notch (a single outing) if the enjoyment disappears or if the child complains of pain.
Weeks 5 to 8

Building skills

  • Habit. Move to an average of about 45 minutes a day, with at least three days that include more vigorous effort and games of jumping, climbing or bodyweight strength (the WHO recommendation).
  • Skill games. Obstacle course at home (crawling, jumping, standing on one foot), throwing at a target, balance games, ball games in pairs. Aim for success at their level, then one notch more.
  • Strength without equipment, with an adult. Bodyweight games, with technique first, without load or repetition targets: this is the logic of supervision described by the 2014 consensus.
  • A supervised activity, on trial. A trial session at a club or in an activity where they can succeed, chosen with them.
  • Mini-test at week 6. Only two tests: the 20 m shuttle run and, depending on age, the flamingo balance or the long jump. Aim: to see whether it is moving, not to get a score.
Weeks 9 to 12

Holding the average, without forcing

  • Habit. Reach about 60 minutes a day on average over the week, counting everything: school, journeys, games, club. A day at 30 minutes and another at 90 count the same.
  • Games. The child chooses the two games of the week. The idea is that they become, in part, the organiser.
  • Full THW test at week 12. Same tests, same conditions, same time of day if possible. Compare with the start, test by test, not on the total alone.
  • Reading the result. Progress on the shuttle run or the balance says that one quality has moved forward. A plateau on one test is information, not a failure. No average gain figure is given here: we have not read a trial that measures it in this type of child over twelve weeks.
Afterwards · Maintenance

Making it last

  • Keep the rituals that held, drop those that did not take. Retest every three to six months, no more often: a child grows, and the norm tables are by age.
  • Gradually hand over: the child suggests, you accompany.
  • If a step was missed, go back to the previous step without experiencing it as a setback.
What this means

The plan is deliberately modest in its steps and patient in its duration. In the adults of the Lally study, a behaviour took 66 days on average to settle in, with wide variation: twelve weeks (84 days) are only a beginning, and the plan is not finished after that. If you manage two things, a regular bedtime with no screen in the bedroom and a daily movement ritual, you have already done the essential.

Common mistakes, warning signs, when to consult

Common mistakes

  • Talking about weight or diets in front of the child.The HAS asks to fight stigmatisation and to support the relationship with the body, in girls as in boys.4
  • Choosing a sport without them.A sense of competence is the probable link with future activity; a sport that is endured damages it.7
  • Turning the test into a grade.It serves to compare yourself with yourself over time, not with a brother or a classmate.
  • Skipping coordination.Only making them run or counting minutes leaves aside the lever most linked to the desire to move more later.7,8
  • Wanting to change everything in one week.One ritual at a time. Duration matters more than the intensity of the start.18
  • Loading strength too fast.Strength is possible, supervised and progressive; overweight young people get injured more often.14
Warning signs: ask for medical advice before increasing effort

What follows is a general reference point, not a diagnosis and not personalised advice. Talk to your doctor or paediatrician if:

  • your child gets out of breath disproportionately compared with others during light effort, or feels palpitations;
  • they have chest pain on exertion, feel faint, dizzy or lose consciousness: these are questions asked by physical activity readiness questionnaires (PAR-Q), originally designed for adults and cited here as a reference point for questions to ask yourself;21
  • they have joint or bone pain that lasts or gets worse with movement (same source);
  • a known heart condition, a chronic illness, a treatment, or any reason to think that physical activity poses a problem (same source);
  • their body-size growth chart in the health record book rises continuously or quickly moves up to a higher band, or if the overweight is marked: in these cases the HAS asks for more frequent follow-up and a full assessment, looking for complications (hypertension, respiratory, orthopaedic, metabolic, psychological problems);4
  • sleep is regularly very short or very long, or there is daytime sleepiness: the 2016 consensus asks to consult in these cases;11
  • distress around the body, food or school (teasing, bullying): the HAS asks for these situations to be assessed.4

When in doubt, the simplest rule is the best: medical advice taken before starting delays the plan by only a few days.

A straight answer to the question

A child aged 6 to 11 who is out of shape does not need a training plan, they need an environment where moving is easy, enjoyable and normal, and a parent who takes part in it. What the research read establishes: the recommended dose is 60 minutes of movement a day on average, with more vigorous and strengthening activities three days a week; coordination in childhood is linked to the desire to move later; sleep and screens weigh on the child's health; the management of overweight is family-based, comprehensive, and must not stigmatise; the average effect of programmes is small, with low certainty of evidence.

What is a suggestion, not tested as it stands: the twelve-week trajectory, the ten-minute steps, the mini-tests, the skill games chosen, the language to use, trying out a club. What remains uncertain: the precise effect of parental involvement (the Cochrane trials find no difference in it), the real share of school and clubs, the speed of progress to expect from the tests in twelve weeks.

For your child, the best starting decision is a modest one: a daily movement ritual, a regular bedtime with no screen in the bedroom, a THW test to place them, and medical advice if a warning sign exists. Then repeat, for months.

Limits

What this article does not say
  • It gives no personalised medical advice and does not replace a paediatrician or a sports doctor.
  • Several data come from adolescents (Tomkinson 9-17 years, Barnett 16 years at follow-up, Carter 6-19 years) or from adults (Lally, Gollwitzer, Michie), not from children aged 6-11.
  • Most of the links cited are associations, not demonstrated effects.
  • The Epstein figure comes from a press release and not from the original paper.
  • The warning signs are general reference points: the full paediatric list was not read.
  • Diet, detailed cardiac safety and the precise role of school are not covered for lack of a source read.

Frequently asked questions

Should my child do sport at a club?

No, not necessarily. The WHO counts all activity in the 60-minute average.1 A club can help if it lets them succeed at movements at their level. Try it before enrolling.

Should I put them on a diet if they are overweight?

Not on your own initiative. The HAS asks for comprehensive, supported care, in which weight loss is not the priority objective in a growing child.4 Talk to their doctor about it.

How often should the THW test be repeated?

Two to three times in twelve weeks (start, mini-test at week 6, full test at week 12), then every three to six months. This is a suggestion: no trial read sets this frequency.

My child refuses to move. What should I do?

Lower the step, not the ambition: a single ritual, a game they choose, no criticism. One study suggests that the sense of competence is linked to future activity; so offer successful challenges first.7 If the refusal is abrupt, accompanied by pain or sadness, consult.
